newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel hopes for fair deal at Cairo conference.
newsitem.headline: Israel hopes for fair deal at Cairo conference.

text.p: Israel hopes to get a square deal at this week's Cairo economic conference despite Arab opposition to the policies of right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Anything less will be an embarrassment to the United States, which lobbied wary Israeli business executives to attend, and to Netanyahu himself -- although a decision to exclude government leaders from the event will effectively keep him away too.

"Go to Cairo, make deals at the conference. It is good for the Jews, it is good for the Arabs, it is good for peace," Netanyahu told the approximately 100-strong delegation of Israeli businessmen and bureaucrats on Thursday.

The Israelis are armed with a 180-page "Programmes for Regional Cooperation" ranging from improving the drinking water in the Gaza Strip to a proposed $5 billion Red Sea-Dead Sea canal to produce electricity -- a project on the books for decades.

Officials and businesspeople from more than 80 countries are expected at the three-day conference opening on Tuesday. Two previous conferences were aimed at integrating Israel into the regional economy after peace deals with the Palestinians.

In Cairo last week, Ahmed Abu el-Kheir, Egypt's foreign ministry coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa Economic Conference, said the absence of progress in Arab-Israeli peace meant key regional projects were unlikely to move forward.

Mohsin al-Balushi, head of Oman's trade representation office in Tel Aviv, said an Israeli-PLO deal on implementing Israel's long-delayed partial troop pullback from the West Bank town of Hebron would break the ice.

"Any breakthrough in the peace process and the negotiations, especially redeployment in Hebron will positively impact the receiving of the Israelis among Omanis and also others -- and the success, of course, of the event in general," he told reporters.
Netanyahu's message to Israel's delegation was, in his words, "very simple".

"We will work in the sphere of peace," Netanyahu said, referring to his government. "You will work to achieve your business profits. I am certain you will find good partners...on the Arab side and I want to wish you success."
Netanyahu also sought to allay Arab apprehensions, voiced after the first two regional economic conferences in Casablanca and Amman, that Israel sought economic domination in the Middle East.

"I know there is always a fear in the Arab world that we aspire to some sort of economic colonisation," he said. "The natural development of the Israeli economy...is in the direction of the Western economies and economic ties with the United States, Western Europe and Asia."
Netanyahu said he was sending his ministers of foreign affairs, finance, trade and industry, transportation and communications to Cairo to "tighten and strengthen" Arab-Israeli relations.
"If you succeed in business, you've earned peace. And if you succeed in peace, you've earned business," he told the delegation.
One senior Israeli cabinet member said "no deal".

National Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon, a former general who led Israeli forces across the Suez Canal in the 1973 Middle East war, ordered ministry personnel not to go to Cairo in protest at Egyptian criticism of Israeli policies.
Dan Propper, head of the Manufacturers' Association of Israel, said he was assured by Egypt's ambassador to Israel and a top Egyptian business leader "we will be very welcome guests".
Propper said he and 30 Israeli manufacturers and industrialists would join 30 Egyptian colleagues for a boat ride on the Nile to discuss business.
"High-ranking political people in Egypt", he said, had invited Israeli business executives to lunch during the conference.
"I suppose that we can all go smiling to Cairo," Propper told the delegation.
